[42](https://docs.rs#42)pub const NON_DUP_MARKER: u8 = u8::MAX;
[43](https://docs.rs#43)
[44](https://docs.rs#44)/// Declare the program entrypoint and set up global handlers.
[45](https://docs.rs#45)///
[46](https://docs.rs#46)/// This macro emits the common boilerplate necessary to begin program
[47](https://docs.rs#47)/// execution, calling a provided function to process the program instruction
[48](https://docs.rs#48)/// supplied by the runtime, and reporting its result to the runtime.
[49](https://docs.rs#49)///
[50](https://docs.rs#50)/// It also sets up a [global allocator] and [panic handler], using the
[51](https://docs.rs#51)/// [`custom_heap_default`] and [`custom_panic_default`] macros.
[52](https://docs.rs#52)///
[53](https://docs.rs#53)/// [`custom_heap_default`]: crate::custom_heap_default
[54](https://docs.rs#54)/// [`custom_panic_default`]: crate::custom_panic_default
[55](https://docs.rs#55)///
[56](https://docs.rs#56)/// [global allocator]: https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/alloc/trait.GlobalAlloc.html
[57](https://docs.rs#57)/// [panic handler]: https://doc.rust-lang.org/nomicon/panic-handler.html
[58](https://docs.rs#58)///
[59](https://docs.rs#59)/// The argument is the name of a function with this type signature:
[60](https://docs.rs#60)///
[61](https://docs.rs#61)/// ```ignore
[62](https://docs.rs#62)/// fn process_instruction(
[63](https://docs.rs#63)///     program_id: &Pubkey,      // Public key of the account the program was loaded into
[64](https://docs.rs#64)///     accounts: &[AccountInfo], // All accounts required to process the instruction
[65](https://docs.rs#65)///     instruction_data: &[u8],  // Serialized instruction-specific data
[66](https://docs.rs#66)/// ) -> ProgramResult;
[67](https://docs.rs#67)/// ```
[68](https://docs.rs#68)///
[69](https://docs.rs#69)/// # Cargo features
[70](https://docs.rs#70)///
[71](https://docs.rs#71)/// This macro emits symbols and definitions that may only be defined once
[72](https://docs.rs#72)/// globally. As such, if linked to other Rust crates it will cause compiler
[73](https://docs.rs#73)/// errors. To avoid this, it is common for Solana programs to define an
[74](https://docs.rs#74)/// optional [Cargo feature] called `no-entrypoint`, and use it to conditionally
[75](https://docs.rs#75)/// disable the `entrypoint` macro invocation, as well as the
[76](https://docs.rs#76)/// `process_instruction` function. See a typical pattern for this in the
[77](https://docs.rs#77)/// example below.
[78](https://docs.rs#78)///
[79](https://docs.rs#79)/// [Cargo feature]: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/features.html
[80](https://docs.rs#80)///
[81](https://docs.rs#81)/// The code emitted by this macro can be customized by adding cargo features
[82](https://docs.rs#82)/// _to your own crate_ (the one that calls this macro) and enabling them:
[83](https://docs.rs#83)///
[84](https://docs.rs#84)/// - If the `custom-heap` feature is defined then the macro will not set up the
[85](https://docs.rs#85)///   global allocator, allowing `entrypoint` to be used with your own
[86](https://docs.rs#86)///   allocator. See documentation for the [`custom_heap_default`] macro for
[87](https://docs.rs#87)///   details of customizing the global allocator.
[88](https://docs.rs#88)///
[89](https://docs.rs#89)/// - If the `custom-panic` feature is defined then the macro will not define a
[90](https://docs.rs#90)///   panic handler, allowing `entrypoint` to be used with your own panic
[91](https://docs.rs#91)///   handler. See documentation for the [`custom_panic_default`] macro for
[92](https://docs.rs#92)///   details of customizing the panic handler.
[93](https://docs.rs#93)///
[94](https://docs.rs#94)/// # Examples
[95](https://docs.rs#95)///
[96](https://docs.rs#96)/// Defining an entrypoint and making it conditional on the `no-entrypoint`
[97](https://docs.rs#97)/// feature. Although the `entrypoint` module is written inline in this example,
[98](https://docs.rs#98)/// it is common to put it into its own file.
[99](https://docs.rs#99)///
[100](https://docs.rs#100)/// ```no_run
[101](https://docs.rs#101)/// #[cfg(not(feature = "no-entrypoint"))]
[102](https://docs.rs#102)/// pub mod entrypoint {
[103](https://docs.rs#103)///
[104](https://docs.rs#104)///     use solana_account_info::AccountInfo;
[105](https://docs.rs#105)///     use solana_program_entrypoint::entrypoint;
[106](https://docs.rs#106)///     use solana_program_entrypoint::ProgramResult;
[107](https://docs.rs#107)///     use solana_msg::msg;
[108](https://docs.rs#108)///     use solana_pubkey::Pubkey;
[109](https://docs.rs#109)///
[110](https://docs.rs#110)///     entrypoint!(process_instruction);
[111](https://docs.rs#111)///
[112](https://docs.rs#112)///     pub fn process_instruction(
[113](https://docs.rs#113)///         program_id: &Pubkey,
[114](https://docs.rs#114)///         accounts: &[AccountInfo],
[115](https://docs.rs#115)///         instruction_data: &[u8],
[116](https://docs.rs#116)///     ) -> ProgramResult {
[117](https://docs.rs#117)///         msg!("Hello world");
[118](https://docs.rs#118)///
[119](https://docs.rs#119)///         Ok(())
[120](https://docs.rs#120)///     }
[121](https://docs.rs#121)///
[122](https://docs.rs#122)/// }
[123](https://docs.rs#123)/// ```
[124](https://docs.rs#124)#[macro_export]
[125](https://docs.rs#125)macro_rules! entrypoint {
[126](https://docs.rs#126)    ($process_instruction:ident) => {
[127](https://docs.rs#127)        /// # Safety
[128](https://docs.rs#128)        #[no_mangle]
[129](https://docs.rs#129)        pub unsafe extern "C" fn entrypoint(input: *mut u8) -> u64 {
[130](https://docs.rs#130)            let (program_id, accounts, instruction_data) = unsafe { $crate::deserialize(input) };
[131](https://docs.rs#131)            match $process_instruction(program_id, &accounts, instruction_data) {
[132](https://docs.rs#132)                Ok(()) => $crate::SUCCESS,
[133](https://docs.rs#133)                Err(error) => error.into(),
[134](https://docs.rs#134)            }
[135](https://docs.rs#135)        }
[136](https://docs.rs#136)        $crate::custom_heap_default!();
[137](https://docs.rs#137)        $crate::custom_panic_default!();
[138](https://docs.rs#138)    };
[139](https://docs.rs#139)}
[140](https://docs.rs#140)
[141](https://docs.rs#141)/// Declare the program entrypoint and set up global handlers.
[142](https://docs.rs#142)///
[143](https://docs.rs#143)/// This is similar to the `entrypoint!` macro, except that it does not perform
[144](https://docs.rs#144)/// any dynamic allocations, and instead writes the input accounts into a pre-
[145](https://docs.rs#145)/// allocated array.
[146](https://docs.rs#146)///
[147](https://docs.rs#147)/// This version reduces compute unit usage by 20-30 compute units per unique
[148](https://docs.rs#148)/// account in the instruction. It may become the default option in a future
[149](https://docs.rs#149)/// release.
[150](https://docs.rs#150)///
[151](https://docs.rs#151)/// For more information about how the program entrypoint behaves and what it
[152](https://docs.rs#152)/// does, please see the documentation for [`entrypoint!`].
[153](https://docs.rs#153)///
[154](https://docs.rs#154)/// NOTE: This entrypoint has a hard-coded limit of 64 input accounts.
[155](https://docs.rs#155)#[macro_export]
[156](https://docs.rs#156)macro_rules! entrypoint_no_alloc {
[157](https://docs.rs#157)    ($process_instruction:ident) => {
[158](https://docs.rs#158)        /// # Safety
[159](https://docs.rs#159)        #[no_mangle]
[160](https://docs.rs#160)        pub unsafe extern "C" fn entrypoint(input: *mut u8) -> u64 {
[161](https://docs.rs#161)            use std::mem::MaybeUninit;
[162](https://docs.rs#162)            // Clippy complains about this because a `const` with interior
[163](https://docs.rs#163)            // mutability `RefCell` should use `static` instead to make it
[164](https://docs.rs#164)            // clear that it can change.
[165](https://docs.rs#165)            // In our case, however, we want to create an array of `AccountInfo`s,
[166](https://docs.rs#166)            // and the only way to do it is through a `const` expression, and
[167](https://docs.rs#167)            // we don't expect to mutate the internals of this `const` type.
[168](https://docs.rs#168)            #[allow(clippy::declare_interior_mutable_const)]
[169](https://docs.rs#169)            const UNINIT_ACCOUNT_INFO: MaybeUninit<$crate::__AccountInfo> =
[170](https://docs.rs#170)                MaybeUninit::<$crate::__AccountInfo>::uninit();
[171](https://docs.rs#171)            const MAX_ACCOUNT_INFOS: usize = 64;
[172](https://docs.rs#172)            let mut accounts = [UNINIT_ACCOUNT_INFO; MAX_ACCOUNT_INFOS];
[173](https://docs.rs#173)            let (program_id, num_accounts, instruction_data) =
[174](https://docs.rs#174)                unsafe { $crate::deserialize_into(input, &mut accounts) };
[175](https://docs.rs#175)            // Use `slice_assume_init_ref` once it's stabilized
[176](https://docs.rs#176)            let accounts = &*(&accounts[..num_accounts]
[177](https://docs.rs#177)                as *const [MaybeUninit<$crate::__AccountInfo<'_>>]
[178](https://docs.rs#178)                as *const [$crate::__AccountInfo<'_>]);
[179](https://docs.rs#179)
[180](https://docs.rs#180)            #[inline(never)]
[181](https://docs.rs#181)            fn call_program(
[182](https://docs.rs#182)                program_id: &$crate::__Pubkey,
[183](https://docs.rs#183)                accounts: &[$crate::__AccountInfo],
[184](https://docs.rs#184)                data: &[u8],
[185](https://docs.rs#185)            ) -> u64 {
[186](https://docs.rs#186)                match $process_instruction(program_id, accounts, data) {
[187](https://docs.rs#187)                    Ok(()) => $crate::SUCCESS,
[188](https://docs.rs#188)                    Err(error) => error.into(),
[189](https://docs.rs#189)                }
[190](https://docs.rs#190)            }
[191](https://docs.rs#191)
[192](https://docs.rs#192)            call_program(&program_id, accounts, &instruction_data)
[193](https://docs.rs#193)        }
[194](https://docs.rs#194)        $crate::custom_heap_default!();
[195](https://docs.rs#195)        $crate::custom_panic_default!();
[196](https://docs.rs#196)    };
[197](https://docs.rs#197)}
[198](https://docs.rs#198)
[199](https://docs.rs#199)/// Define the default global allocator.
[200](https://docs.rs#200)///
[201](https://docs.rs#201)/// The default global allocator is enabled only if the calling crate has not
[202](https://docs.rs#202)/// disabled it using [Cargo features] as described below. It is only defined
[203](https://docs.rs#203)/// for [BPF] targets.
[204](https://docs.rs#204)///
[205](https://docs.rs#205)/// [Cargo features]: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/features.html
[206](https://docs.rs#206)/// [BPF]: https://solana.com/docs/programs/faq#berkeley-packet-filter-bpf
[207](https://docs.rs#207)///
[208](https://docs.rs#208)/// # Cargo features
[209](https://docs.rs#209)///
[210](https://docs.rs#210)/// A crate that calls this macro can provide its own custom heap
[211](https://docs.rs#211)/// implementation, or allow others to provide their own custom heap
[212](https://docs.rs#212)/// implementation, by adding a `custom-heap` feature to its `Cargo.toml`. After
[213](https://docs.rs#213)/// enabling the feature, one may define their own [global allocator] in the
[214](https://docs.rs#214)/// standard way.
[215](https://docs.rs#215)///
[216](https://docs.rs#216)/// [global allocator]: https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/alloc/trait.GlobalAlloc.html
[217](https://docs.rs#217)///
[218](https://docs.rs#218)#[macro_export]
[219](https://docs.rs#219)macro_rules! custom_heap_default {
[220](https://docs.rs#220)    () => {
[221](https://docs.rs#221)        #[cfg(all(not(feature = "custom-heap"), target_os = "solana"))]
[222](https://docs.rs#222)        #[global_allocator]
[223](https://docs.rs#223)        static A: $crate::BumpAllocator = unsafe {
[224](https://docs.rs#224)            $crate::BumpAllocator::with_fixed_address_range(
[225](https://docs.rs#225)                $crate::HEAP_START_ADDRESS as usize,
[226](https://docs.rs#226)                $crate::HEAP_LENGTH,
[227](https://docs.rs#227)            )
[228](https://docs.rs#228)        };
[229](https://docs.rs#229)    };
[230](https://docs.rs#230)}
[231](https://docs.rs#231)
[232](https://docs.rs#232)/// Define the default global panic handler.
[233](https://docs.rs#233)///
[234](https://docs.rs#234)/// This must be used if the [`entrypoint`] macro is not used, and no other
[235](https://docs.rs#235)/// panic handler has been defined; otherwise a program will crash without an
[236](https://docs.rs#236)/// explicit panic message.
[237](https://docs.rs#237)///
[238](https://docs.rs#238)/// The default global allocator is enabled only if the calling crate has not
[239](https://docs.rs#239)/// disabled it using [Cargo features] as described below. It is only defined
[240](https://docs.rs#240)/// for [BPF] targets.
[241](https://docs.rs#241)///
[242](https://docs.rs#242)/// [Cargo features]: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/features.html
[243](https://docs.rs#243)/// [BPF]: https://solana.com/docs/programs/faq#berkeley-packet-filter-bpf
[244](https://docs.rs#244)///
[245](https://docs.rs#245)/// # Cargo features
[246](https://docs.rs#246)///
[247](https://docs.rs#247)/// A crate that calls this macro can provide its own custom panic handler, or
[248](https://docs.rs#248)/// allow others to provide their own custom panic handler, by adding a
[249](https://docs.rs#249)/// `custom-panic` feature to its `Cargo.toml`. After enabling the feature, one
[250](https://docs.rs#250)/// may define their own panic handler.
[251](https://docs.rs#251)///
[252](https://docs.rs#252)/// A good way to reduce the final size of the program is to provide a
[253](https://docs.rs#253)/// `custom_panic` implementation that does nothing. Doing so will cut ~25kb
[254](https://docs.rs#254)/// from a noop program. That number goes down the more the programs pulls in
[255](https://docs.rs#255)/// Rust's standard library for other purposes.
[256](https://docs.rs#256)///
[257](https://docs.rs#257)/// # Defining a panic handler for Solana
[258](https://docs.rs#258)///
[259](https://docs.rs#259)/// _The mechanism for defining a Solana panic handler is different [from most
[260](https://docs.rs#260)/// Rust programs][rpanic]._
[261](https://docs.rs#261)///
[262](https://docs.rs#262)/// [rpanic]: https://doc.rust-lang.org/nomicon/panic-handler.html
[263](https://docs.rs#263)///
[264](https://docs.rs#264)/// To define a panic handler one must define a `custom_panic` function
[265](https://docs.rs#265)/// with the `#[no_mangle]` attribute, as below:
[266](https://docs.rs#266)///
[267](https://docs.rs#267)/// ```ignore
[268](https://docs.rs#268)/// #[cfg(all(feature = "custom-panic", target_os = "solana"))]
[269](https://docs.rs#269)/// #[no_mangle]
[270](https://docs.rs#270)/// fn custom_panic(info: &core::panic::PanicInfo<'_>) {
[271](https://docs.rs#271)///     $crate::msg!("{}", info);
[272](https://docs.rs#272)/// }
[273](https://docs.rs#273)/// ```
[274](https://docs.rs#274)#[macro_export]
[275](https://docs.rs#275)macro_rules! custom_panic_default {
[276](https://docs.rs#276)    () => {
[277](https://docs.rs#277)        #[cfg(all(not(feature = "custom-panic"), target_os = "solana"))]
[278](https://docs.rs#278)        #[no_mangle]
[279](https://docs.rs#279)        fn custom_panic(info: &core::panic::PanicInfo<'_>) {
[280](https://docs.rs#280)            if let Some(mm) = info.message().as_str() {
[281](https://docs.rs#281)                unsafe {
[282](https://docs.rs#282)                    $crate::__log(mm.as_ptr(), mm.len() as u64);
[283](https://docs.rs#283)                }
[284](https://docs.rs#284)            }
[285](https://docs.rs#285)
[286](https://docs.rs#286)            if let Some(loc) = info.location() {
[287](https://docs.rs#287)                unsafe {
[288](https://docs.rs#288)                    $crate::__panic(
[289](https://docs.rs#289)                        loc.file().as_ptr(),
[290](https://docs.rs#290)                        loc.file().len() as u64,
[291](https://docs.rs#291)                        loc.line() as u64,
[292](https://docs.rs#292)                        loc.column() as u64,
[293](https://docs.rs#293)                    )
[294](https://docs.rs#294)                }
[295](https://docs.rs#295)            }
[296](https://docs.rs#296)        }
[297](https://docs.rs#297)    };
[298](https://docs.rs#298)}
[299](https://docs.rs#299)
[300](https://docs.rs#300)/// The bump allocator used as the default rust heap when running programs.
[301](https://docs.rs#301)pub struct BumpAllocator {
[302](https://docs.rs#302)    start: usize,
[303](https://docs.rs#303)    len: usize,
[304](https://docs.rs#304)}
[305](https://docs.rs#305)
[306](https://docs.rs#306)impl BumpAllocator {
[307](https://docs.rs#307)    /// Creates the allocator tied to a provided slice.
[308](https://docs.rs#308)    /// This will not initialize the provided memory, except for the first
[309](https://docs.rs#309)    /// bytes where the pointer is stored.
[310](https://docs.rs#310)    ///
[311](https://docs.rs#311)    /// # Safety
[312](https://docs.rs#312)    /// As long as BumpAllocator or any of its allocations are alive,
[313](https://docs.rs#313)    /// writing into or deallocating the arena will cause UB.
[314](https://docs.rs#314)    ///
[315](https://docs.rs#315)    /// Integer arithmetic in this global allocator implementation is safe when
[316](https://docs.rs#316)    /// operating on the prescribed `HEAP_START_ADDRESS` and `HEAP_LENGTH`. Any
[317](https://docs.rs#317)    /// other use may overflow and is thus unsupported and at one's own risk.
[318](https://docs.rs#318)    #[inline]
[319](https://docs.rs#319)    #[allow(clippy::arithmetic_side_effects)]
[320](https://docs.rs#320)    pub unsafe fn new(arena: &mut [u8]) -> Self {
[321](https://docs.rs#321)        debug_assert!(
[322](https://docs.rs#322)            arena.len() > size_of::<usize>(),
[323](https://docs.rs#323)            "Arena should be larger than usize"
[324](https://docs.rs#324)        );
[325](https://docs.rs#325)
[326](https://docs.rs#326)        // create a pointer to the start of the arena
[327](https://docs.rs#327)        // that will hold an address of the byte following free space
[328](https://docs.rs#328)        let pos_ptr = arena.as_mut_ptr() as *mut usize;
[329](https://docs.rs#329)        // initialize the data there
[330](https://docs.rs#330)        *pos_ptr = pos_ptr as usize + arena.len();
[331](https://docs.rs#331)
[332](https://docs.rs#332)        Self {
[333](https://docs.rs#333)            start: pos_ptr as usize,
[334](https://docs.rs#334)            len: arena.len(),
[335](https://docs.rs#335)        }
[336](https://docs.rs#336)    }
[337](https://docs.rs#337)
[338](https://docs.rs#338)    /// Creates the allocator tied to specific range of addresses.
[339](https://docs.rs#339)    ///
[340](https://docs.rs#340)    /// # Safety
[341](https://docs.rs#341)    /// This is unsafe in most situations, unless you are totally sure that the
[342](https://docs.rs#342)    /// provided start address and length can be written to by the allocator,
[343](https://docs.rs#343)    /// and that the memory will be usable for the lifespan of the allocator.
[344](https://docs.rs#344)    ///
[345](https://docs.rs#345)    /// For Solana on-chain programs, a certain address range is reserved, so
[346](https://docs.rs#346)    /// the allocator can be given those addresses.
[347](https://docs.rs#347)    pub const unsafe fn with_fixed_address_range(start: usize, len: usize) -> Self {
[348](https://docs.rs#348)        Self { start, len }
[349](https://docs.rs#349)    }
[350](https://docs.rs#350)}
[351](https://docs.rs#351)
[352](https://docs.rs#352)/// Integer arithmetic in this global allocator implementation is safe when
[353](https://docs.rs#353)/// operating on the prescribed `HEAP_START_ADDRESS` and `HEAP_LENGTH`. Any
[354](https://docs.rs#354)/// other use may overflow and is thus unsupported and at one's own risk.
[355](https://docs.rs#355)#[allow(clippy::arithmetic_side_effects)]
[356](https://docs.rs#356)unsafe impl std::alloc::GlobalAlloc for BumpAllocator {
[357](https://docs.rs#357)    #[inline]
[358](https://docs.rs#358)    unsafe fn alloc(&self, layout: Layout) -> *mut u8 {
[359](https://docs.rs#359)        let pos_ptr = self.start as *mut usize;
[360](https://docs.rs#360)        let mut pos = *pos_ptr;
[361](https://docs.rs#361)        if pos == 0 {
[362](https://docs.rs#362)            // First time, set starting position
[363](https://docs.rs#363)            pos = self.start + self.len;
[364](https://docs.rs#364)        }
[365](https://docs.rs#365)        pos = pos.saturating_sub(layout.size());
[366](https://docs.rs#366)        pos &= !(layout.align().wrapping_sub(1));
[367](https://docs.rs#367)        if pos < self.start + size_of::<*mut u8>() {
[368](https://docs.rs#368)            return null_mut();
[369](https://docs.rs#369)        }
[370](https://docs.rs#370)        *pos_ptr = pos;
[371](https://docs.rs#371)        pos as *mut u8
[372](https://docs.rs#372)    }
[373](https://docs.rs#373)    #[inline]
[374](https://docs.rs#374)    unsafe fn dealloc(&self, _: *mut u8, _: Layout) {
[375](https://docs.rs#375)        // I'm a bump allocator, I don't free
[376](https://docs.rs#376)    }
[377](https://docs.rs#377)}
[378](https://docs.rs#378)
[379](https://docs.rs#379)/// `assert_eq(std::mem::align_of::<u128>(), 8)` is true for BPF but not for some host machines
[380](https://docs.rs#380)pub const BPF_ALIGN_OF_U128: usize = 8;
[381](https://docs.rs#381)
[382](https://docs.rs#382)#[allow(clippy::arithmetic_side_effects)]
[383](https://docs.rs#383)#[inline(always)] // this reduces CU usage
[384](https://docs.rs#384)unsafe fn deserialize_instruction_data<'a>(input: *mut u8, mut offset: usize) -> (&'a [u8], usize) {
[385](https://docs.rs#385)    #[allow(clippy::cast_ptr_alignment)]
[386](https://docs.rs#386)    let instruction_data_len = *(input.add(offset) as *const u64) as usize;
[387](https://docs.rs#387)    offset += size_of::<u64>();
[388](https://docs.rs#388)
[389](https://docs.rs#389)    let instruction_data = { from_raw_parts(input.add(offset), instruction_data_len) };
[390](https://docs.rs#390)    offset += instruction_data_len;
[391](https://docs.rs#391)
[392](https://docs.rs#392)    (instruction_data, offset)
[393](https://docs.rs#393)}
[394](https://docs.rs#394)
[395](https://docs.rs#395)#[allow(clippy::arithmetic_side_effects)]
[396](https://docs.rs#396)#[inline(always)] // this reduces CU usage by half!
[397](https://docs.rs#397)unsafe fn deserialize_account_info<'a>(
[398](https://docs.rs#398)    input: *mut u8,
[399](https://docs.rs#399)    mut offset: usize,
[400](https://docs.rs#400)) -> (AccountInfo<'a>, usize) {
[401](https://docs.rs#401)    #[allow(clippy::cast_ptr_alignment)]
[402](https://docs.rs#402)    let is_signer = *(input.add(offset) as *const u8) != 0;
[403](https://docs.rs#403)    offset += size_of::<u8>();
[404](https://docs.rs#404)
[405](https://docs.rs#405)    #[allow(clippy::cast_ptr_alignment)]
[406](https://docs.rs#406)    let is_writable = *(input.add(offset) as *const u8) != 0;
[407](https://docs.rs#407)    offset += size_of::<u8>();
[408](https://docs.rs#408)
[409](https://docs.rs#409)    #[allow(clippy::cast_ptr_alignment)]
[410](https://docs.rs#410)    let executable = *(input.add(offset) as *const u8) != 0;
[411](https://docs.rs#411)    offset += size_of::<u8>();
[412](https://docs.rs#412)
[413](https://docs.rs#413)    // The original data length is stored here because these 4 bytes were
[414](https://docs.rs#414)    // originally only used for padding and served as a good location to
[415](https://docs.rs#415)    // track the original size of the account data in a compatible way.
[416](https://docs.rs#416)    let original_data_len_offset = offset;
[417](https://docs.rs#417)    offset += size_of::<u32>();
[418](https://docs.rs#418)
[419](https://docs.rs#419)    let key: &Pubkey = &*(input.add(offset) as *const Pubkey);
[420](https://docs.rs#420)    offset += size_of::<Pubkey>();
[421](https://docs.rs#421)
[422](https://docs.rs#422)    let owner: &Pubkey = &*(input.add(offset) as *const Pubkey);
[423](https://docs.rs#423)    offset += size_of::<Pubkey>();
[424](https://docs.rs#424)
[425](https://docs.rs#425)    #[allow(clippy::cast_ptr_alignment)]
[426](https://docs.rs#426)    let lamports = &mut *(input.add(offset) as *mut u64);
[427](https://docs.rs#427)    offset += size_of::<u64>();
[428](https://docs.rs#428)
[429](https://docs.rs#429)    #[allow(clippy::cast_ptr_alignment)]
[430](https://docs.rs#430)    let data_len = *(input.add(offset) as *const u64) as usize;
[431](https://docs.rs#431)    offset += size_of::<u64>();
[432](https://docs.rs#432)
[433](https://docs.rs#433)    // Store the original data length for detecting invalid reallocations and
[434](https://docs.rs#434)    // requires that MAX_PERMITTED_DATA_LENGTH fits in a u32
[435](https://docs.rs#435)    *(input.add(original_data_len_offset) as *mut u32) = data_len as u32;
[436](https://docs.rs#436)
[437](https://docs.rs#437)    let data = from_raw_parts_mut(input.add(offset), data_len);
[438](https://docs.rs#438)    // rent epoch is not deserialized, so skip it
[439](https://docs.rs#439)    offset += data_len + MAX_PERMITTED_DATA_INCREASE + size_of::<u64>();
[440](https://docs.rs#440)    offset += (offset as *const u8).align_offset(BPF_ALIGN_OF_U128); // padding
[441](https://docs.rs#441)
[442](https://docs.rs#442)    (
[443](https://docs.rs#443)        AccountInfo::new(
[444](https://docs.rs#444)            key,
[445](https://docs.rs#445)            is_signer,
[446](https://docs.rs#446)            is_writable,
[447](https://docs.rs#447)            lamports,
[448](https://docs.rs#448)            data,
[449](https://docs.rs#449)            owner,
[450](https://docs.rs#450)            executable,
[451](https://docs.rs#451)        ),
[452](https://docs.rs#452)        offset,
[453](https://docs.rs#453)    )
[454](https://docs.rs#454)}
[455](https://docs.rs#455)
[456](https://docs.rs#456)/// Deserialize the input arguments
[457](https://docs.rs#457)///
[458](https://docs.rs#458)/// The integer arithmetic in this method is safe when called on a buffer that was
[459](https://docs.rs#459)/// serialized by runtime. Use with buffers serialized otherwise is unsupported and
[460](https://docs.rs#460)/// done at one's own risk.
[461](https://docs.rs#461)///
[462](https://docs.rs#462)/// # Safety
[463](https://docs.rs#463)#[allow(clippy::arithmetic_side_effects)]
[464](https://docs.rs#464)pub unsafe fn deserialize<'a>(input: *mut u8) -> (&'a Pubkey, Vec<AccountInfo<'a>>, &'a [u8]) {
[465](https://docs.rs#465)    let mut offset: usize = 0;
[466](https://docs.rs#466)
[467](https://docs.rs#467)    // Number of accounts present
[468](https://docs.rs#468)
[469](https://docs.rs#469)    #[allow(clippy::cast_ptr_alignment)]
[470](https://docs.rs#470)    let num_accounts = *(input.add(offset) as *const u64) as usize;
[471](https://docs.rs#471)    offset += size_of::<u64>();
[472](https://docs.rs#472)
[473](https://docs.rs#473)    // Account Infos
[474](https://docs.rs#474)
[475](https://docs.rs#475)    let mut accounts = Vec::with_capacity(num_accounts);
[476](https://docs.rs#476)    for _ in 0..num_accounts {
[477](https://docs.rs#477)        let dup_info = *(input.add(offset) as *const u8);
[478](https://docs.rs#478)        offset += size_of::<u8>();
[479](https://docs.rs#479)        if dup_info == NON_DUP_MARKER {
[480](https://docs.rs#480)            let (account_info, new_offset) = deserialize_account_info(input, offset);
[481](https://docs.rs#481)            offset = new_offset;
[482](https://docs.rs#482)            accounts.push(account_info);
[483](https://docs.rs#483)        } else {
[484](https://docs.rs#484)            offset += 7; // padding
[485](https://docs.rs#485)
[486](https://docs.rs#486)            // Duplicate account, clone the original
[487](https://docs.rs#487)            accounts.push(accounts[dup_info as usize].clone());
[488](https://docs.rs#488)        }
[489](https://docs.rs#489)    }
[490](https://docs.rs#490)
[491](https://docs.rs#491)    // Instruction data
[492](https://docs.rs#492)
[493](https://docs.rs#493)    let (instruction_data, new_offset) = deserialize_instruction_data(input, offset);
[494](https://docs.rs#494)    offset = new_offset;
[495](https://docs.rs#495)
[496](https://docs.rs#496)    // Program Id
[497](https://docs.rs#497)
[498](https://docs.rs#498)    let program_id: &Pubkey = &*(input.add(offset) as *const Pubkey);
[499](https://docs.rs#499)
[500](https://docs.rs#500)    (program_id, accounts, instruction_data)
[501](https://docs.rs#501)}
[502](https://docs.rs#502)
[503](https://docs.rs#503)/// Deserialize the input arguments
[504](https://docs.rs#504)///
[505](https://docs.rs#505)/// Differs from `deserialize` by writing the account infos into an uninitialized
[506](https://docs.rs#506)/// slice, which provides better performance, roughly 30 CUs per unique account
[507](https://docs.rs#507)/// provided to the instruction.
[508](https://docs.rs#508)///
[509](https://docs.rs#509)/// Panics if the input slice is not large enough.
[510](https://docs.rs#510)///
[511](https://docs.rs#511)/// The integer arithmetic in this method is safe when called on a buffer that was
[512](https://docs.rs#512)/// serialized by runtime. Use with buffers serialized otherwise is unsupported and
[513](https://docs.rs#513)/// done at one's own risk.
[514](https://docs.rs#514)///
[515](https://docs.rs#515)/// # Safety
[516](https://docs.rs#516)#[allow(clippy::arithmetic_side_effects)]
[517](https://docs.rs#517)pub unsafe fn deserialize_into<'a>(
[518](https://docs.rs#518)    input: *mut u8,
[519](https://docs.rs#519)    accounts: &mut [MaybeUninit<AccountInfo<'a>>],
[520](https://docs.rs#520)) -> (&'a Pubkey, usize, &'a [u8]) {
[521](https://docs.rs#521)    let mut offset: usize = 0;
[522](https://docs.rs#522)
[523](https://docs.rs#523)    // Number of accounts present
[524](https://docs.rs#524)
[525](https://docs.rs#525)    #[allow(clippy::cast_ptr_alignment)]
[526](https://docs.rs#526)    let num_accounts = *(input.add(offset) as *const u64) as usize;
[527](https://docs.rs#527)    offset += size_of::<u64>();
[528](https://docs.rs#528)
[529](https://docs.rs#529)    if num_accounts > accounts.len() {
[530](https://docs.rs#530)        panic!(
[531](https://docs.rs#531)            "{} accounts provided, but only {} are supported",
[532](https://docs.rs#532)            num_accounts,
[533](https://docs.rs#533)            accounts.len()
[534](https://docs.rs#534)        );
[535](https://docs.rs#535)    }
[536](https://docs.rs#536)
[537](https://docs.rs#537)    // Account Infos
[538](https://docs.rs#538)
[539](https://docs.rs#539)    for i in 0..num_accounts {
[540](https://docs.rs#540)        let dup_info = *(input.add(offset) as *const u8);
[541](https://docs.rs#541)        offset += size_of::<u8>();
[542](https://docs.rs#542)        if dup_info == NON_DUP_MARKER {
[543](https://docs.rs#543)            let (account_info, new_offset) = deserialize_account_info(input, offset);
[544](https://docs.rs#544)            offset = new_offset;
[545](https://docs.rs#545)            accounts[i].write(account_info);
[546](https://docs.rs#546)        } else {
[547](https://docs.rs#547)            offset += 7; // padding
[548](https://docs.rs#548)
[549](https://docs.rs#549)            // Duplicate account, clone the original
[550](https://docs.rs#550)            accounts[i].write(accounts[dup_info as usize].assume_init_ref().clone());
[551](https://docs.rs#551)        }
[552](https://docs.rs#552)    }
[553](https://docs.rs#553)
[554](https://docs.rs#554)    // Instruction data
[555](https://docs.rs#555)
[556](https://docs.rs#556)    let (instruction_data, new_offset) = deserialize_instruction_data(input, offset);
[557](https://docs.rs#557)    offset = new_offset;
[558](https://docs.rs#558)
[559](https://docs.rs#559)    // Program Id
[560](https://docs.rs#560)
[561](https://docs.rs#561)    let program_id: &Pubkey = &*(input.add(offset) as *const Pubkey);
[562](https://docs.rs#562)
[563](https://docs.rs#563)    (program_id, num_accounts, instruction_data)
[564](https://docs.rs#564)}
[565](https://docs.rs#565)
[566](https://docs.rs#566)#[cfg(test)]
[567](https://docs.rs#567)mod test {
[568](https://docs.rs#568)    use {super::*, std::alloc::GlobalAlloc};
[569](https://docs.rs#569)
[570](https://docs.rs#570)    #[test]
[571](https://docs.rs#571)    fn test_bump_allocator() {
[572](https://docs.rs#572)        // alloc the entire
[573](https://docs.rs#573)        {
[574](https://docs.rs#574)            let mut heap = [0u8; 128];
[575](https://docs.rs#575)            let allocator = unsafe { BumpAllocator::new(&mut heap) };
[576](https://docs.rs#576)            for i in 0..128 - size_of::<*mut u8>() {
[577](https://docs.rs#577)                let ptr = unsafe {
[578](https://docs.rs#578)                    allocator.alloc(Layout::from_size_align(1, size_of::<u8>()).unwrap())
[579](https://docs.rs#579)                };
[580](https://docs.rs#580)                assert_eq!(ptr as usize, heap.as_ptr() as usize + heap.len() - 1 - i);
[581](https://docs.rs#581)            }
[582](https://docs.rs#582)            assert_eq!(null_mut(), unsafe {
[583](https://docs.rs#583)                allocator.alloc(Layout::from_size_align(1, 1).unwrap())
[584](https://docs.rs#584)            });
[585](https://docs.rs#585)        }
[586](https://docs.rs#586)        // check alignment
[587](https://docs.rs#587)        {

# custom_heap_default in solana_program_entrypoint - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/solana-program-entrypoint/latest/target-redirect/solana_program_entrypoint/macro.custom_heap_default.html

```
macro_rules! custom_heap_default {
    () => { ... };
}
```
## Expand description

Define the default global allocator.

The default global allocator is enabled only if the calling crate has not
disabled it using [Cargo features](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/features.html) as described below. It is only defined
for [BPF](https://solana.com/docs/programs/faq#berkeley-packet-filter-bpf) targets.

[§](https://docs.rs#cargo-features)Cargo features

A crate that calls this macro can provide its own custom heap
implementation, or allow others to provide their own custom heap
implementation, by adding a `custom-heap` feature to its `Cargo.toml`. After
enabling the feature, one may define their own [global allocator](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/alloc/trait.GlobalAlloc.html) in the
standard way.

---

# custom_panic_default in solana_program_entrypoint - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/solana-program-entrypoint/latest/target-redirect/solana_program_entrypoint/macro.custom_panic_default.html

```
macro_rules! custom_panic_default {
    () => { ... };
}
```
## Expand description

Define the default global panic handler.

This must be used if the [ entrypoint](https://docs.rs/macro.entrypoint.html) macro is not used, and no other
panic handler has been defined; otherwise a program will crash without an
explicit panic message.

The default global allocator is enabled only if the calling crate has not
disabled it using [Cargo features](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/features.html) as described below. It is only defined
for [BPF](https://solana.com/docs/programs/faq#berkeley-packet-filter-bpf) targets.

[§](https://docs.rs#cargo-features)Cargo features

A crate that calls this macro can provide its own custom panic handler, or
allow others to provide their own custom panic handler, by adding a
`custom-panic` feature to its `Cargo.toml`. After enabling the feature, one
may define their own panic handler.

A good way to reduce the final size of the program is to provide a
`custom_panic` implementation that does nothing. Doing so will cut ~25kb
from a noop program. That number goes down the more the programs pulls in
Rust’s standard library for other purposes.

[§](https://docs.rs#defining-a-panic-handler-for-solana)Defining a panic handler for Solana

*The mechanism for defining a Solana panic handler is different  from most
Rust programs.*

To define a panic handler one must define a `custom_panic` function
with the `#[no_mangle]` attribute, as below:

---

# entrypoint in solana_program_entrypoint - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/solana-program-entrypoint/latest/target-redirect/solana_program_entrypoint/macro.entrypoint.html

```
macro_rules! entrypoint {
    ($process_instruction:ident) => { ... };
}
```
## Expand description

Declare the program entrypoint and set up global handlers.

This macro emits the common boilerplate necessary to begin program execution, calling a provided function to process the program instruction supplied by the runtime, and reporting its result to the runtime.

It also sets up a [global allocator](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/alloc/trait.GlobalAlloc.html) and [panic handler](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nomicon/panic-handler.html), using the
[ custom_heap_default](https://docs.rs/macro.custom_heap_default.html) and

[macros.](https://docs.rs/macro.custom_panic_default.html)

`custom_panic_default`The argument is the name of a function with this type signature:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
fn process_instruction(
    program_id: &Pubkey,      // Public key of the account the program was loaded into
    accounts: &[AccountInfo], // All accounts required to process the instruction
    instruction_data: &[u8],  // Serialized instruction-specific data
) -> ProgramResult;
```
[§](https://docs.rs#cargo-features)Cargo features

This macro emits symbols and definitions that may only be defined once
globally. As such, if linked to other Rust crates it will cause compiler
errors. To avoid this, it is common for Solana programs to define an
optional [Cargo feature](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/features.html) called `no-entrypoint`, and use it to conditionally
disable the `entrypoint` macro invocation, as well as the
`process_instruction` function. See a typical pattern for this in the
example below.

The code emitted by this macro can be customized by adding cargo features
*to your own crate* (the one that calls this macro) and enabling them:

-
If the `custom-heap`feature is defined then the macro will not set up the global allocator, allowing`entrypoint`to be used with your own allocator. See documentation for the`custom_heap_default`
-
If the `custom-panic`feature is defined then the macro will not define a panic handler, allowing`entrypoint`to be used with your own panic handler. See documentation for the`custom_panic_default`

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

Defining an entrypoint and making it conditional on the `no-entrypoint`
feature. Although the `entrypoint` module is written inline in this example,
it is common to put it into its own file.

```
#[cfg(not(feature = "no-entrypoint"))]
pub mod entrypoint {
    use solana_account_info::AccountInfo;
    use solana_program_entrypoint::entrypoint;
    use solana_program_entrypoint::ProgramResult;
    use solana_msg::msg;
    use solana_pubkey::Pubkey;
    entrypoint!(process_instruction);
    pub fn process_instruction(
        program_id: &Pubkey,
        accounts: &[AccountInfo],
        instruction_data: &[u8],
    ) -> ProgramResult {
        msg!("Hello world");
        Ok(())
    }
}
```

---

# entrypoint_no_alloc in solana_program_entrypoint - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/solana-program-entrypoint/latest/target-redirect/solana_program_entrypoint/macro.entrypoint_no_alloc.html

```
macro_rules! entrypoint_no_alloc {
    ($process_instruction:ident) => { ... };
}
```
## Expand description

Declare the program entrypoint and set up global handlers.

This is similar to the `entrypoint!` macro, except that it does not perform
any dynamic allocations, and instead writes the input accounts into a pre-
allocated array.

This version reduces compute unit usage by 20-30 compute units per unique account in the instruction. It may become the default option in a future release.

For more information about how the program entrypoint behaves and what it
does, please see the documentation for [ entrypoint!](https://docs.rs/macro.entrypoint.html).

NOTE: This entrypoint has a hard-coded limit of 64 input accounts.

---

# BumpAllocator in solana_program_entrypoint - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/solana-program-entrypoint/latest/target-redirect/solana_program_entrypoint/struct.BumpAllocator.html

`pub struct BumpAllocator { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

The bump allocator used as the default rust heap when running programs.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/solana_program_entrypoint/lib.rs.html#306-350)[§](https://docs.rs#impl-BumpAllocator)### impl [BumpAllocator](https://docs.rs/struct.BumpAllocator.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/solana_program_entrypoint/lib.rs.html#306-350)

[§](https://docs.rs#impl-BumpAllocator)

### impl [BumpAllocator](https://docs.rs/struct.BumpAllocator.html)

Creates the allocator tied to a provided slice. This will not initialize the provided memory, except for the first bytes where the pointer is stored.

[§](https://docs.rs#safety)Safety

As long as BumpAllocator or any of its allocations are alive, writing into or deallocating the arena will cause UB.

Integer arithmetic in this global allocator implementation is safe when
operating on the prescribed `HEAP_START_ADDRESS` and `HEAP_LENGTH`. Any
other use may overflow and is thus unsupported and at one’s own risk.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/solana_program_entrypoint/lib.rs.html#347-349)#### pub const unsafe fn [with_fixed_address_range](https://docs.rs#method.with_fixed_address_range)(start: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html), len: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)) -> Self

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/solana_program_entrypoint/lib.rs.html#347-349)

#### pub const unsafe fn [with_fixed_address_range](https://docs.rs#method.with_fixed_address_range)(start: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html), len: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)) -> Self

Creates the allocator tied to specific range of addresses.

[§](https://docs.rs#safety-1)Safety

This is unsafe in most situations, unless you are totally sure that the provided start address and length can be written to by the allocator, and that the memory will be usable for the lifespan of the allocator.

For Solana on-chain programs, a certain address range is reserved, so the allocator can be given those addresses.

#### pub fn [try_borrow_data](https://docs.rs#method.try_borrow_data)(&self) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[Ref](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cell/struct.Ref.html)<'_, &mut [[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)]>, [ProgramError](https://docs.rs/solana-program-error/3.0.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/solana_program_error/enum.ProgramError.html)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/solana-account-info/3.0.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/solana_account_info/lib.rs.html#132)

#### pub fn [try_borrow_mut_data](https://docs.rs#method.try_borrow_mut_data)(
    &self,
) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[RefMut](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cell/struct.RefMut.html)<'_, &'a mut [[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)]>, [ProgramError](https://docs.rs/solana-program-error/3.0.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/solana_program_error/enum.ProgramError.html)>

Resize the account’s data: Either truncating or zero extending.

Note:  Account data can be increased within a single call by up to
`solana_program::entrypoint::MAX_PERMITTED_DATA_INCREASE` bytes.

[§](https://docs.rs#safety-1)Safety

This method makes assumptions about the layout and location of memory
referenced by `AccountInfo` fields. It should only be called for
instances of `AccountInfo` that were created by the runtime and received
in the `process_instruction` entrypoint of a program.

[Source](https://docs.rs/solana-account-info/3.0.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/solana_account_info/lib.rs.html#185)

[Source](https://docs.rs/solana-account-info/3.0.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/solana_account_info/lib.rs.html#195-203)

# deserialize_into in solana_program_entrypoint - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/solana-program-entrypoint/latest/target-redirect/solana_program_entrypoint/fn.deserialize_into.html

```
pub unsafe fn deserialize_into<'a>(
    input:
```
[*mut ](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.pointer.html)[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html),
    accounts: &mut [[MaybeUninit](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/mem/maybe_uninit/union.MaybeUninit.html)<[AccountInfo](https://docs.rs/struct.__AccountInfo.html)<'a>>],
) -> (&'a [Pubkey](https://docs.rs/struct.__Pubkey.html), [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html), &'a [[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)])## Expand description

Deserialize the input arguments

Differs from `deserialize` by writing the account infos into an uninitialized
slice, which provides better performance, roughly 30 CUs per unique account
provided to the instruction.

Panics if the input slice is not large enough.

The integer arithmetic in this method is safe when called on a buffer that was serialized by runtime. Use with buffers serialized otherwise is unsupported and done at one’s own risk.

---

# clap - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/clap

## Expand description

Command Line Argument Parser for Rust

Quick Links:

- Derive [tutorial](https://docs.rs/_derive/_tutorial/index.html)and[reference](https://docs.rs/_derive/index.html)
- Builder [tutorial](https://docs.rs/_tutorial/index.html)and[reference](https://docs.rs/struct.Command.html)
- [Cookbook](https://docs.rs/_cookbook/index.html)
- [CLI Concepts](https://docs.rs/_concepts/index.html)
- [FAQ](https://docs.rs/_faq/index.html)
- [Discussions](https://github.com/clap-rs/clap/discussions)
- [CHANGELOG](https://github.com/clap-rs/clap/blob/v4.6.1/CHANGELOG.md)(includes major version migration guides)

[§](https://docs.rs#aspirations)Aspirations

- Out of the box, users get a polished CLI experience
- Including common argument behavior, help generation, suggested fixes for users, colored output, [shell completions](https://github.com/clap-rs/clap/tree/master/clap_complete), etc

- Including common argument behavior, help generation, suggested fixes for users, colored output,
- Flexible enough to port your existing CLI interface
- However, we won’t necessarily streamline support for each use case

- Reasonable parse performance
- Resilient maintainership, including
- Willing to break compatibility rather than batching up breaking changes in large releases
- Leverage feature flags to keep to one active branch
- Being under [WG-CLI](https://github.com/rust-cli/team/)to increase the bus factor

- We follow semver and will wait about 6-9 months between major breaking changes
- We will support the last two minor Rust releases (MSRV, currently 1.74)

While these aspirations can be at odds with fast build times and low binary
size, we will still strive to keep these reasonable for the flexibility you
get.  Check out the
[argparse-benchmarks](https://github.com/rust-cli/argparse-benchmarks-rs) for
CLI parsers optimized for other use cases.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

Run

`$ cargo add clap --features derive`*(See also  feature flag reference)*

Then define your CLI in `main.rs`:

```
use clap::Parser;
/// Simple program to greet a person
#[derive(Parser, Debug)]
#[command(version, about, long_about = None)]
struct Args {
    /// Name of the person to greet
    #[arg(short, long)]
    name: String,
    /// Number of times to greet
    #[arg(short, long, default_value_t = 1)]
    count: u8,
}
fn main() {
    let args = Args::parse();
    for _ in 0..args.count {
        println!("Hello {}!", args.name);
    }
}
```
And try it out:

```
$ demo --help
A simple to use, efficient, and full-featured Command Line Argument Parser
Usage: demo[EXE] [OPTIONS] --name <NAME>
Options:
  -n, --name <NAME>    Name of the person to greet
  -c, --count <COUNT>  Number of times to greet [default: 1]
  -h, --help           Print help
  -V, --version        Print version
$ demo --name Me
Hello Me!
```
*(version number and  .exe extension on windows replaced by placeholders)*

See also the derive [tutorial](https://docs.rs/_derive/_tutorial/index.html) and [reference](https://docs.rs/_derive/index.html)

[§](https://docs.rs#related-projects)Related Projects

Augment clap:

- [wild](https://crates.io/crates/wild)for supporting wildcards (- `*`) on Windows like you do Linux
- [argfile](https://crates.io/crates/argfile)for loading additional arguments from a file (aka response files)
- [shadow-rs](https://crates.io/crates/shadow-rs)for generating- `Command::long_version`
- [clap_mangen](https://crates.io/crates/clap_mangen)for generating man page source (roff)
- [clap_complete](https://crates.io/crates/clap_complete)for shell completion support
- [clap-i18n-richformatter](https://crates.io/crates/clap-i18n-richformatter)for i18n support with- `clap::error::RichFormatter`

CLI Helpers

- [clio](https://crates.io/crates/clio)for reading/writing to files specified as arguments
- [clap-verbosity-flag](https://crates.io/crates/clap-verbosity-flag)
- [clap-cargo](https://crates.io/crates/clap-cargo)
- [colorchoice-clap](https://crates.io/crates/colorchoice-clap)

Testing

- `trycmd`
- `snapbox`
- `assert_cmd`- `assert_fs`

Documentation:

# clap - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2

## Expand description

`clap` is a simple-to-use, efficient, and full-featured library for parsing command line
arguments and subcommands when writing console/terminal applications.

`clap` is used to parse *and validate* the string of command line arguments provided by the user
at runtime. You provide the list of valid possibilities, and `clap` handles the rest. This means
you focus on your *applications* functionality, and less on the parsing and validating of
arguments.

`clap` also provides the traditional version and help switches (or flags) ‘for free’ meaning
automatically with no configuration. It does this by checking the list of valid possibilities you
supplied and adding only the ones you haven’t already defined. If you are using subcommands,
`clap` will also auto-generate a `help` subcommand for you in addition to the traditional flags.

Once `clap` parses the user provided string of arguments, it returns the matches along with any
applicable values. If the user made an error or typo, `clap` informs them of the mistake and
exits gracefully (or returns a `Result` type and allows you to perform any clean up prior to
exit). Because of this, you can make reasonable assumptions in your code about the validity of
the arguments.

The following examples show a quick example of some of the very basic functionality of `clap`.
For more advanced usage, such as requirements, conflicts, groups, multiple values and
occurrences see the [documentation](https://docs.rs/clap/), [examples/](https://github.com/clap-rs/clap/tree/v2.34.0/examples) directory of
this repository or the [video tutorials](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLza5oFLQGTl2Z5T8g1pRkIynR3E0_pc7U).

**NOTE:** All of these examples are functionally the same, but show different styles in which to
use `clap`

The first example shows a method that allows more advanced configuration options (not shown in this small example), or even dynamically generating arguments when desired. The downside is it’s more verbose.

```
// (Full example with detailed comments in examples/01b_quick_example.rs)
//
// This example demonstrates clap's full 'builder pattern' style of creating arguments which is
// more verbose, but allows easier editing, and at times more advanced options, or the possibility
// to generate arguments dynamically.
extern crate clap;
use clap::{Arg, App, SubCommand};
fn main() {
    let matches = App::new("My Super Program")
                          .version("1.0")
                          .author("Kevin K. <kbknapp@gmail.com>")
                          .about("Does awesome things")
                          .arg(Arg::with_name("config")
                               .short("c")
                               .long("config")
                               .value_name("FILE")
                               .help("Sets a custom config file")
                               .takes_value(true))
                          .arg(Arg::with_name("INPUT")
                               .help("Sets the input file to use")
                               .required(true)
                               .index(1))
                          .arg(Arg::with_name("v")
                               .short("v")
                               .multiple(true)
                               .help("Sets the level of verbosity"))
                          .subcommand(SubCommand::with_name("test")
                                      .about("controls testing features")
                                      .version("1.3")
                                      .author("Someone E. <someone_else@other.com>")
                                      .arg(Arg::with_name("debug")
                                          .short("d")
                                          .help("print debug information verbosely")))
                          .get_matches();
    // Gets a value for config if supplied by user, or defaults to "default.conf"
    let config = matches.value_of("config").unwrap_or("default.conf");
    println!("Value for config: {}", config);
    // Calling .unwrap() is safe here because "INPUT" is required (if "INPUT" wasn't
    // required we could have used an 'if let' to conditionally get the value)
    println!("Using input file: {}", matches.value_of("INPUT").unwrap());
    // Vary the output based on how many times the user used the "verbose" flag
    // (i.e. 'myprog -v -v -v' or 'myprog -vvv' vs 'myprog -v'
    match matches.occurrences_of("v") {
        0 => println!("No verbose info"),
        1 => println!("Some verbose info"),
        2 => println!("Tons of verbose info"),
        3 | _ => println!("Don't be crazy"),
    }
    // You can handle information about subcommands by requesting their matches by name
    // (as below), requesting just the name used, or both at the same time
    if let Some(matches) = matches.subcommand_matches("test") {
        if matches.is_present("debug") {
            println!("Printing debug info...");
        } else {
            println!("Printing normally...");
        }
    }
    // more program logic goes here...
}
```
The next example shows a far less verbose method, but sacrifices some of the advanced
configuration options (not shown in this small example). This method also takes a *very* minor
runtime penalty.

```
// (Full example with detailed comments in examples/01a_quick_example.rs)
//
// This example demonstrates clap's "usage strings" method of creating arguments
// which is less verbose
extern crate clap;
use clap::{Arg, App, SubCommand};
fn main() {
    let matches = App::new("myapp")
                          .version("1.0")
                          .author("Kevin K. <kbknapp@gmail.com>")
                          .about("Does awesome things")
                          .args_from_usage(
                              "-c, --config=[FILE] 'Sets a custom config file'
                              <INPUT>              'Sets the input file to use'
                              -v...                'Sets the level of verbosity'")
                          .subcommand(SubCommand::with_name("test")
                                      .about("controls testing features")
                                      .version("1.3")
                                      .author("Someone E. <someone_else@other.com>")
                                      .arg_from_usage("-d, --debug 'Print debug information'"))
                          .get_matches();
    // Same as previous example...
}
```
This third method shows how you can use a YAML file to build your CLI and keep your Rust source tidy or support multiple localized translations by having different YAML files for each localization.

First, create the `cli.yml` file to hold your CLI options, but it could be called anything we
like:

```
name: myapp
version: "1.0"
author: Kevin K. <kbknapp@gmail.com>
about: Does awesome things
args:
    - config:
        short: c
        long: config
        value_name: FILE
        help: Sets a custom config file
        takes_value: true
    - INPUT:
        help: Sets the input file to use
        required: true
        index: 1
    - verbose:
        short: v
        multiple: true
        help: Sets the level of verbosity
subcommands:
    - test:
        about: controls testing features
        version: "1.3"
        author: Someone E. <someone_else@other.com>
        args:
            - debug:
                short: d
                help: print debug information
```
Since this feature requires additional dependencies that not everyone may want, it is *not*
compiled in by default and we need to enable a feature flag in Cargo.toml:

Simply change your `clap = "~2.27.0"` to `clap = {version = "~2.27.0", features = ["yaml"]}`.

At last we create our `main.rs` file just like we would have with the previous two examples:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
// (Full example with detailed comments in examples/17_yaml.rs)
//
// This example demonstrates clap's building from YAML style of creating arguments which is far
// more clean, but takes a very small performance hit compared to the other two methods.
#[macro_use]
extern crate clap;
use clap::App;
fn main() {
    // The YAML file is found relative to the current file, similar to how modules are found
    let yaml = load_yaml!("cli.yml");
    let matches = App::from_yaml(yaml).get_matches();
    // Same as previous examples...
}
```
Finally there is a macro version, which is like a hybrid approach offering the speed of the builder pattern (the first example), but without all the verbosity.

```
#[macro_use]
extern crate clap;
fn main() {
    let matches = clap_app!(myapp =>
        (version: "1.0")
        (author: "Kevin K. <kbknapp@gmail.com>")
        (about: "Does awesome things")
        (@arg CONFIG: -c --config +takes_value "Sets a custom config file")
        (@arg INPUT: +required "Sets the input file to use")
        (@arg debug: -d ... "Sets the level of debugging information")
        (@subcommand test =>
            (about: "controls testing features")
            (version: "1.3")
            (author: "Someone E. <someone_else@other.com>")
            (@arg verbose: -v --verbose "Print test information verbosely")
        )
    ).get_matches();
    // Same as before...
}
```
If you were to compile any of the above programs and run them with the flag `--help` or `-h` (or
`help` subcommand, since we defined `test` as a subcommand) the following would be output

```
$ myprog --help
My Super Program 1.0
Kevin K. <kbknapp@gmail.com>
Does awesome things
USAGE:
    MyApp [FLAGS] [OPTIONS] <INPUT> [SUBCOMMAND]
FLAGS:
    -h, --help       Prints this message
    -v               Sets the level of verbosity
    -V, --version    Prints version information
OPTIONS:
    -c, --config <FILE>    Sets a custom config file
ARGS:
    INPUT    The input file to use
SUBCOMMANDS:
    help    Prints this message
    test    Controls testing features
```
**NOTE:** You could also run `myapp test --help` to see similar output and options for the
`test` subcommand.

To try out the pre-built example, use the following steps:

- Clone the repository `$ git clone https://github.com/clap-rs/clap && cd clap-rs/tests`
- Compile the example `$ cargo build --release`
- Run the help info `$ ./target/release/claptests --help`
- Play with the arguments!

To test out `clap`’s default auto-generated help/version follow these steps:

- Create a new cargo project `$ cargo new fake --bin && cd fake`
- Add `clap`to your`Cargo.toml`

```
[dependencies]
clap = "2"
```
- Add the following to your `src/main.rs`

```
extern crate clap;
use clap::App;
fn main() {
  App::new("fake").version("v1.0-beta").get_matches();
}
```
- Build your program `$ cargo build --release`
- Run with help or version `$ ./target/release/fake --help`or`$ ./target/release/fake --version`

For full usage, add `clap` as a dependency in your `Cargo.toml` (it is **highly** recommended to
use the `~major.minor.patch` style versions in your `Cargo.toml`, for more information see
[Compatibility Policy](https://docs.rs#compatibility-policy)) to use from crates.io:

```
[dependencies]
clap = "~2.27.0"
```
Or get the latest changes from the master branch at github:

```
[dependencies.clap]
git = "https://github.com/clap-rs/clap.git"
```
Add `extern crate clap;` to your crate root.

Define a list of valid arguments for your program (see the
[documentation](https://docs.rs/clap/) or [examples/](https://github.com/clap-rs/clap/tree/v2.34.0/examples) directory of this repo)

Then run `cargo build` or `cargo update && cargo build` for your project.

- `suggestions`: Turns on the- `Did you mean '--myoption'?`feature for when users make typos. (builds dependency- `strsim`)
- `color`: Turns on colored error messages. This feature only works on non-Windows OSs. (builds dependency- `ansi-term`and- `atty`)
- `wrap_help`: Wraps the help at the actual terminal width when available, instead of 120 characters. (builds dependency- `textwrap`with feature- `term_size`)

To disable these, add this to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[dependencies.clap]
version = "~2.27.0"
default-features = false
```
You can also selectively enable only the features you’d like to include, by adding:

```
[dependencies.clap]
version = "~2.27.0"
default-features = false
# Cherry-pick the features you'd like to use
features = [ "suggestions", "color" ]
```
- **“yaml”**: Enables building CLIs from YAML documents. (builds dependency- `yaml-rust`)
- **“unstable”**: Enables unstable- `clap`features that may change from release to release

The following graphic depicts `clap`s dependency graph (generated using
[cargo-graph](https://github.com/kbknapp/cargo-graph)).

- **Dashed**Line: Optional dependency
- **Red**Color:- **NOT**included by default (must use cargo- `features`to enable)
- **Blue**Color: Dev dependency, only used while developing.

Another really great way to help is if you find an interesting, or helpful way in which to use
`clap`. You can either add it to the [examples/](https://github.com/clap-rs/clap/tree/v2.34.0/examples) directory, or file an issue and tell
me. I’m all about giving credit where credit is due :)

To test with all features both enabled and disabled, you can run theese commands:

```
$ cargo test --no-default-features
$ cargo test --features "yaml unstable"
```
Alternatively, if you have [ just](https://github.com/casey/just) installed you can run the
prebuilt recipes.

*Not*using

`just` is perfectly fine as well, it simply bundles commands
automatically.For example, to test the code, as above simply run:

```
$ just run-tests
```
From here on, I will list the appropriate `cargo` command as well as the `just` command.

Sometimes it’s helpful to only run a subset of the tests, which can be done via:

```
$ cargo test --test <test_name>
# Or
$ just run-test <test_name>
```
During the CI process `clap` runs against many different lints using
[ clippy](https://github.com/Manishearth/rust-clippy). In order to check if these lints pass on
your own computer prior to submitting a PR you’ll need a nightly compiler.

In order to check the code for lints run either:

```
$ rustup override add nightly
$ cargo build --features lints
$ rustup override remove
# Or
$ just lint
```
Another helpful technique is to see the `clap` debug output while developing features. In order
to see the debug output while running the full test suite or individual tests, run:

```
$ cargo test --features debug
# Or for individual tests
$ cargo test --test <test_name> --features debug
# The corresponding just command for individual debugging tests is:
$ just debug <test_name>
```
There are a few goals of `clap` that I’d like to maintain throughout contributions. If your
proposed changes break, or go against any of these goals we’ll discuss the changes further
before merging (but will *not* be ignored, all contributes are welcome!). These are by no means
hard-and-fast rules, as I’m no expert and break them myself from time to time (even if by
mistake or ignorance).

- Remain backwards compatible when possible
- If backwards compatibility *must*be broken, use deprecation warnings if at all possible before removing legacy code - This does not apply for security concerns

- If backwards compatibility
- Parse arguments quickly
- Parsing of arguments shouldn’t slow down usage of the main program - This is also true of
generating help and usage information (although *slightly*less stringent, as the program is about to exit)

- Parsing of arguments shouldn’t slow down usage of the main program - This is also true of
generating help and usage information (although
- Try to be cognizant of memory usage
- Once parsing is complete, the memory footprint of `clap`should be low since the main program is the star of the show

- Once parsing is complete, the memory footprint of
- `panic!`on- *developer*error, exit gracefully on- *end-user*error

Because `clap` takes `SemVer` and compatibility seriously, this is the official policy regarding
breaking changes and previous versions of Rust.

`clap` will pin the minimum required version of Rust to the CI builds. Bumping the minimum
version of Rust is considered a minor breaking change, meaning *at a minimum* the minor version
of `clap` will be bumped.

In order to keep from being surprised by breaking changes, it is **highly** recommended to use
the `~major.minor.patch` style in your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[dependencies] clap = "~2.27.0"
```
This will cause *only* the patch version to be updated upon a `cargo update` call, and therefore
cannot break due to new features, or bumped minimum versions of Rust.

`clap` will officially support current stable Rust, minus two releases, but may work with prior
releases as well. For example, current stable Rust at the time of this writing is 1.21.0,
meaning `clap` is guaranteed to compile with 1.19.0 and beyond. At the 1.22.0 release, `clap`
will be guaranteed to compile with 1.20.0 and beyond, etc.

Upon bumping the minimum version of Rust (assuming it’s within the stable-2 range), it *must* be
clearly annotated in the `CHANGELOG.md`

`clap` is licensed under the MIT license. Please read the [LICENSE-MIT](https://github.com/clap-rs/clap/blob/v2.34.0/LICENSE-MIT) file in
this repository for more information.

- `pub use fmt::Format;`

- Counts the number of comma-delimited expressions passed to it. The result is a compile-time evaluable expression, suitable for use as a static array size, or the value of a`const`.
- Allows you to build the`App`instance from your Cargo.toml at compile time.
- Build`App`,`Arg`s,`SubCommand`s and`Group`s with Usage-string like input but without the associated parsing runtime cost.
- Allows you to pull the authors for the app from your Cargo.toml at compile time in the form:`"author1 lastname <author1@example.com>:author2 lastname <author2@example.com>"`
- Allows you to pull the description from your Cargo.toml at compile time.
- Allows you to pull the name from your Cargo.toml at compile time.
- Allows you to pull the version from your Cargo.toml at compile time as`MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH_PKGVERSION_PRE`
- A convenience macro for loading the YAML file at compile time (relative to the current file, like modules work). That YAML object can then be passed to this function.
- Convenience macro getting a typed value`T`where`T`implements`std::str::FromStr``Result<T,String>`which allows you as the developer to decide what you’d like to do on a failed parse. There are two types of errors, parse failures and those where the argument wasn’t present (such as a non-required argument). You can use it to get a single value, or a iterator as with the`ArgMatches::values_of`
- Convenience macro getting a typed value`Vec<T>``T`implements`std::str::FromStr``clap::Result<Vec<T>>`

- Used to create a representation of a command line program and all possible command line arguments. Application settings are set using the “builder pattern” with the`App::get_matches`
- The abstract representation of a command line argument. Used to set all the options and relationships that define a valid argument for the program.
- `ArgGroup`s are a family of related- [arguments](https://docs.rs/struct.Arg.html)and way for you to express, “Any of these arguments”. By placing arguments in a logical group, you can create easier requirement and exclusion rules instead of having to list each argument individually, or when you want a rule to apply “any but not all” arguments.
- Command Line Argument Parser Error
- The abstract representation of a command line subcommand.

- Command line argument parser kind of error
- Describes which shell to produce a completions file for
